question: What is the difference between `NULL`, `0`, and `nullptr`?

scenes.sub: Two integers in disguise, and one real null pointer.
scenes.say: NULL, zero, and null p t r. All three can give you a null pointer. Only one of them is actually a pointer.

scenes.head: Three ways to say “points to nothing”

panels.code:
int* a = 0;         // literal zero
int* b = NULL;      // a macro: 0 or 0L
int* c = nullptr;   // C++11: a real null pointer

scenes.say: Zero is just an integer literal, that the language allows to convert into a null pointer. NULL is a macro inherited from C, usually defined as zero, or zero L. Still an integer. Only null p t r, added in C plus plus eleven, is a real null pointer, with its own type: std nullptr t.

scenes.head: Why it matters: overloading
scenes.say: Why does it matter? Overloading. Calling f with zero picks the int version, of course. Calling f with NULL, you'd expect the pointer version, but you get the int version, or a compile error saying the call is ambiguous. null p t r can only convert to a pointer, so it always picks the pointer version.

scenes.head: Where each one can go
scenes.say: Picture the conversions. Zero and NULL are integers, that can also sneak into pointers. null p t r converts to any pointer type, but never to an integer. One meaning, no surprises.

scenes.head: Same story with auto

steps.cue: auto of null p t r

scenes.say: The same thing happens with auto. auto of NULL gives you an integer, not a pointer. auto of null p t r gives a null pointer type. And comparing against null p t r makes your intent obvious to every reader.

lines: 0: an int literal that can also convert to a pointer.
NULL: a C macro for 0 (or 0L). Still an integer.
nullptr (C++11): a true null pointer, type std::nullptr_t. Always use it.
scenes.say: Zero is an integer that can become a pointer. NULL is a macro for zero, still an integer. null p t r is a true null pointer. In modern C plus plus, always use it.
